content:
Earlier, I replaced a battery-powered push lawn mower with a robotic lawn mower that can be controlled via iPhone. Users need to manually drive the lawn mower around the yard using iPhone to create a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will automatically perform mowing tasks according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after weeks of testing, I think it may be a simpler choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic map creation

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I tested earlier this year lies in how each understands the yard environment.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the lawn mower along the boundary using iPhone to create the initial map.

On the other hand, the TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the lawn mower to automatically map the lawn without the need to pre-lay boundary wires or install additional RTK antennas.

Automatically creating the initial map takes longer. However, I think this method may be easier for users who are not familiar with tech products.

To verify this, I specifically asked my mother, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my assistance. She said everything worked well. But I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to manually drive the robot along the entire boundary and mark areas to avoid one by one.

When automatically drawing the map, there were some minor issues in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbor's lawn, so TerraMow initially included part of my neighbor's lawn in the map.

I resolved the issue by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if the lawn doesn't have a clearly visible boundary, the initial map-drawing process may require a bit more effort.

Viewing through the lawn mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favorite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the lawn mower sees while working.

During testing, I used the iPhone mirroring feature on my Mac to open this view in a large window. This allowed me to work indoors while watching from the robot's first-person perspective as it navigated the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes using the robot more enjoyable, and occasionally explains why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 doesn't have a similar camera view feature.

Other than that, the two iPhone apps have many similar design elements. Both let you schedule work, adjust mowing style, divide zones, mark locations to avoid, and remotely control the lawn mower.

Speaking of the last feature, TerraMow has a particularly clever design. In addition to the standard left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed operation mode. You can hold the iPhone as usual and control the lawn mower using only your thumb.

Manually driving the lawn mower with iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should automatically complete its work according to a preset schedule without human intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick controls are surprisingly practical when trimming areas the robot missed.

Sometimes, I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot by telepathy (it's a strange feeling). I can walk while letting the iPhone hang at my side, and with just a gentle nudge of my thumb, the robot drives toward me.

Every robotic lawn mower app should emulate this control method.

A more aggressive lawn mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is loud, but the difference between the two is obvious. The Anthbot can run so quietly that you almost forget it's still mowing, even when it's working at night with its headlights on.

Since TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging station, whereas Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I relied on it to mow for several consecutive weeks without ever needing to intervene personally.

When adaptive mapping becomes too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up sometimes backfires.

The lawn mower continuously updates its map based on what it sees. Saving these updates after each session takes time, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

After several days of continuous rain, I encountered an interesting situation. Puddles formed in parts of the yard, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next mowing session.

Weeds began growing taller in the circular area it skipped. Over time, the lawn mower seemed to treat that patch of tall grass as a place to continue avoiding, even after the ground dried out, that patch remained excluded from the work area.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the lawn mower over that tall grass and trim it. Once the area returned to normal lawn condition, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regularly trimming the edges can also help TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. If the grass in areas with unclear boundaries grows too tall, the system may treat it as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach is less adaptive and relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work but avoids the map 'changing its mind' because of a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

After trying both systems, for most people, I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, pre-laying boundary wires is completely out of the question, and installing an RTK base station also means dealing with another piece of hardware that needs to be positioned, powered, and maintained. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't perfect. Initial map drawing takes longer, invisible property boundaries require manual correction, and its adaptive behavior once mistook tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, quality real-time camera view, and the best manual control features I've seen in a robotic lawn mower app.

I personally enjoy working on the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot frees up more time for me to focus on landscaping, trimming edges, and other detailed work while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs well enough for me to recommend it, especially for those who want to use a robotic mower but don't want the hassle of laying wires, installing RTK antennas, or walking around the entire yard manually holding an iPhone.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, and the website also offers a $200 coupon. You can also find this product on TerraMow's official website.
